content.text: {"answers":[{"id":"p1","answer":"The docs state that processing order is determined by `iter_params_for_processing()` ([src/click/core.py:116-141]()), which places eager parameters first, then non-eager parameters in the order they were encountered on the command line (the parser's `order` list), then any remaining parameters in declaration order. For `hello` invoked as `--count=3` with a prompted `--name`, that means the eager `--help` option is handled first, then `count` (the only option actually given on the command line), then `name` (remaining, in declaration order), which is where the prompt happens. The documentation does not show the actual README example or its decorator order, so the exact declaration order of `--count`/`--name` is an assumption on my part; the ordering *rule* is as described."},{"id":"p2","answer":"The documentation describes `_OptionParser.parse_args()` returning a three-tuple `(opts, largs, order)` built up in `_ParsingState`: `opts` is a dict of parsed values, `largs` the leftover/non-option args, and `order` the list of parameters in the order they were encountered. For `--count=3`, `_process_opts` splits on `=`, normalizes `--count`, looks it up in `_long_opt`, injects `\"3\"` back into `rargs`, and stores the raw string. So `opts` would be roughly `{'count': '3'}` (the parser's `dest` for that option), `largs` empty, and `order` containing the `count` Parameter object. The docs do not show a literal transcript of this call, so the precise key spelling is inferred from the described mechanism rather than quoted."},{"id":"p3","answer":"Per the `ParameterSource` enum ([src/click/core.py:143-167]()) and the resolution pipeline, `count` is recorded as `ParameterSource.COMMANDLINE` because it was given on the command line. `name` is recorded as `ParameterSource.PROMPT`, because the CLI, environment variable, default_map and default lookups all fail and the value is finally obtained via the interactive prompt — prompting is an explicit tracked source. The help option has `expose_value=False`, so nothing is stored for it in `ctx.params`; the documentation does not say what, if anything, is recorded in `ctx._parameter_source` for a non-exposed eager flag, so I can't state that definitively."},{"id":"p4","answer":"Click infers the type from the default value when `type` is not given ([docs/options.rst:103-106](), [tests/test_options.py:571-578]()). So `--count` with an integer default gets `click.INT` (the `IntParamType`), and `--name` with a string default (or no default) gets `click.STRING`. The callback therefore receives `count` as a Python `int` — `3` — since `ParamType.convert()` ran on the raw `'3'` string during `type_cast_value()`. (The docs don't include the README source, so this assumes `--count` has an int default such as `1`; if it had no default at all it would fall back to `STRING`.)"},{"id":"p5","answer":"The documentation doesn't settle the prompt question directly. What it does establish: an invalid value for an int option raises `BadParameter`, a `UsageError` subclass with `exit_code = 2`, and the error is printed to stderr in the form `Usage: ...` + `Try 'hello --help' for help.` + `Error: Invalid value for '--count': 'x' is not a valid integer.` ([src/click/exceptions.py:56-135](), [tests/test_basic.py:444-454]()). Whether the `--name` prompt still fires depends on processing order: since `count` is processed before `name` (it was given on the command line, `name` is a remaining parameter), the failure occurs first and the prompt is never reached — but the docs do not explicitly confirm this interaction, so treat the \"no prompt\" part as inference. Exit code is 2."},{"id":"p6","answer":"The help option is added during `make_context()` ([src/click/core.py:1013-1029]()) rather than being a user-declared parameter; it is injected into the parameter list surfaced by `get_params(ctx)` and is not part of the statically declared `hello.params` from the decorators. Its default declaration is `--help` with `is_flag=True`, `is_eager=True`, `expose_value=False` ([src/click/decorators.py:527-551]()). Because `expose_value=False`, nothing is stored for it; `ctx.params` ends up with just `{'count': ..., 'name': ...}`. The documentation does not give the internal attribute name under which the injected option is stored, so I can't name it."},{"id":"p7","answer":"The callback returns normally, `Context.__exit__` runs `close()` which drains the `_exit_stack` (close callbacks and `with_resource` managers), and `main()` returns exit code 0 ([src/click/core.py:1036-1150](), [src/click/core.py:481-493]()). In the `Result` object: `exit_code == 0`, `exception is None`, `exc_info is None`, and `return_value` holds whatever the command returned — but note `return_value` is only meaningfully populated when invoked with `standalone_mode=False` ([tests/test_testing.py:404-414]()); in default standalone mode `Command.main()` ignores the return value ([docs/commands.rst:384-429]()), so for a plain `runner.invoke(hello, ...)` the docs don't guarantee a useful `return_value`."},{"id":"p8","answer":"`click.prompt()` writes the prompt text via `echo()` and defaults to stdout (`err=False`); the typed value itself is consumed from the mocked stdin and is not written by Click to stdout unless the runner was created with `echo_stdin=True` ([src/click/termui.py:139-147](), [tests/test_testing.py:30-86]()). Under `CliRunner`, `result.stdout` holds stdout only, `result.stderr` holds stderr only, and `result.output` is the interleaved mix as a user would see it ([src/click/testing.py:151-227](), [tests/test_testing.py:344-369]()). Since nothing here goes to stderr, `stderr` is empty and `output == stdout`. The documentation does not explain how the literal text `Your name: Click` (including the echoed `Click`) appears without `echo_stdin=True`, so I can't fully account for that line."},{"id":"g1","answer":"The documentation describes the feature-switch pattern — several options sharing one name, each with its own `flag_value`, e.g. `@click.option('--upper', 'transformation', flag_value='upper', default=True)` and `@click.option('--lower', 'transformation', flag_value='lower')` ([docs/options.md:322-363]()) — and notes that when `default=True` is paired with a `flag_value`, the parameter receives the `flag_value` rather than boolean `True`. Beyond that, the docs do not spell out the precise rule for which option's value wins in `ctx.params[name]`, nor the tie-break when two share a name and both fall back to defaults. I can't answer that part from what's here."},{"id":"g2","answer":"`UNSET` (defined in `src/click/_utils.py`) is purely internal: the guarantee is that user-facing code never sees it. It is converted to `None` when values pass through `Context.invoke()` ([src/click/core.py:800-814]()), and `type_cast_value()` short-circuits on `UNSET` so custom `ParamType`/`Parameter` subclasses never receive it — the test suite asserts exactly this (`assert value is not UNSET` inside an overridden `type_cast_value`, [tests/test_options.py:1028-1049]()). Enforcement points are therefore `Parameter.type_cast_value` ([src/click/core.py:2715-2739]()) and `Context.invoke`. Required parameters whose value is still `UNSET` after resolution raise `MissingParameter` in `process_value()`."},{"id":"g3","answer":"The documentation does not describe any validation performed by `Command.get_params`. What it does say about `get_params(ctx)` is that it returns the command's parameters (including the injected help option) and is used by `format_options()` and `get_usage_pieces()` ([src/click/core.py:1074-1113](), [src/click/core.py:1040-1057]()). Validation errors that are documented happen at parameter *construction* time instead — e.g. `TypeError` for `Argument(..., multiple=True)` or `nargs` with a tuple type, and `ValueError` for a required+deprecated argument ([tests/test_arguments.py:489-501](), [tests/test_arguments.py:331-333]()). So I can't confirm any name/spelling checks in `get_params` from these docs."},{"id":"g4","answer":"The documentation describes only one capture strategy for `CliRunner`: the `isolation()` context manager replaces `sys.stdin`/`sys.stdout`/`sys.stderr` with `_NamedTextIOWrapper` objects over in-memory `BytesIO`-based streams managed by `StreamMixer`/`BytesIOCopy`, so stdout and stderr are captured separately while also being copied into a combined `output` buffer ([src/click/testing.py:279-432](), [src/click/testing.py:88-112]()). There is no mention of a second, file-descriptor-level capture mode, nor of behaviour for code calling `sys.stdout.fileno()`. I can't answer the comparison you're asking about from this documentation."},{"id":"g5","answer":"`Command.main()` catches and formats exceptions according to `standalone_mode` ([src/click/core.py:1036-1150]()). Documented mapping: `Exit` → the code carried by the exception; `Abort` → 1; `UsageError` → 2 (prints usage + help hint + error); `ClickException` → 1 (prints the formatted message); `NoArgsIsHelpError` → 2 (prints help to stderr); any other exception → 1. `EOFError`/`KeyboardInterrupt` exit 1 in standalone mode. With `standalone_mode=True` the handler calls `sys.exit(code)`; with `standalone_mode=False` exceptions are re-raised to the caller instead of being caught and formatted, and the command's return value is propagated rather than discarded ([docs/commands.rst:384-429]())."},{"id":"g6","answer":"`Parameter.consume_value(ctx, opts)` checks sources in priority order ([src/click/core.py:2468-2527]()): (1) the parsed command-line `opts`; (2) the environment variable via `resolve_envvar_value(ctx)` (explicit `envvar`, or an auto-generated name from `Context.auto_envvar_prefix`); (3) `Context.default_map` via `ctx.lookup_default(name)`; (4) the parameter's own `default` via `get_default(ctx)`; and for options, (5) an interactive prompt. If none supply a value it stays `UNSET`. As of Click 8.0+, an empty-string environment variable (`\"\"`) is treated as if the variable were not set, so resolution falls through to the next source ([CHANGES.rst:590-598](), [tests/test_options.py:383-393]())."},{"id":"g7","answer":"Reading `Option.default` gives you the raw stored attribute, which may be a callable (a dynamic default), may be an un-normalized iterable for `multiple=True`/`nargs`, and crucially ignores `Context.default_map`. `Parameter.get_default(ctx, call=True)` ([src/click/core.py:2858-2890]()) consults `ctx.lookup_default()` first — so a default_map entry overrides the attribute — and calls callable defaults to produce the actual value. It is also the path through which type-consistent values (e.g. the tuple for `multiple=True`) are produced; the docs show `opt.get_default(ctx) == (1, 2)` for `default=(1, 2)` ([tests/test_options.py:571-578]()). For flag options there is additional interaction between `default` and `flag_value` that `get_default` accounts for ([CHANGES.rst:24-33]())."}]}
